title: Achan (Joshua 7)
hook: one man's hidden theft brings trouble on everyone

segments.voice: Yesterday, teruah, the shout that brought Jericho's walls down after the silence. Your line was circle, then shout. Today, what someone carried out of Jericho.

The book tells the secret before anyone in the story knows it. Chapter seven opens: the children of Israel broke faith, because a man named Achan took things from Jericho that were forbidden, and hid them. Joshua has no idea. He sends a small force up to Ai, a little town, an easy win after Jericho. They run. Men die on the slope. And the hearts of the people melt like water, the same words Rahab used about Jericho's fear. Joshua tears his clothes and lies on his face before the ark until evening.
screen: `THE READER KNOWS FIRST.` → `DEFEAT AT AI.` → `JOSHUA ON HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: God's answer is short: "Israel hath sinned." Not Achan. Israel. One man took, one man hid, and the text names the whole people. It's uncomfortable on purpose: in this story nobody is purely private. What one person buries reaches everyone. Then comes the search, and it's slow. The tribes come forward, and one tribe is taken by lot. Then that tribe's families, then its households, then its men, one by one. The circle narrows, and all through it Achan says nothing. Only when the lot falls on him by name does Joshua speak to him, and gently: my son, give glory to God, tell me what you've done, hide it not from me. And Achan tells it, step by step. I saw. I coveted. I took. They're hidden in the ground, inside my tent. Saw, wanted, took, hid: a whole hidden thing in one sentence. The ending is hard, and the text doesn't soften it: Achan and his household are stoned in a valley that gets the name Achor, trouble. The rabbis read the chapter's first verdict closely. The Talmud notices the word Israel: even when Israel sins, it says, it is still Israel. Achan's wrong is called the people's, and the people keep their name.
screen: `ISRAEL HATH SINNED.` · `THE CIRCLE NARROWS.` · `SAW, COVETED, TOOK, HID.` · then, large: `STILL ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Let something come up that you've kept buried: a thing you took, a word you didn't say, a habit you'd rather no one saw. Don't argue with it or fix it now; just name it silently, to no one but you, the way Achan finally did: I saw, I wanted, I took, I hid. Then breathe out, and let it be known, at least by you.
Achan. The man who hid what he took from Jericho, whose silence brought trouble on everyone, whose people are still called Israel. Today's word.
Your line: one hidden thing affects all. And the people keep their name. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish confession on Yom Kippur is said in the plural, "we have sinned", by the whole congregation together, and the Talmud's reading of Achan's story is cited for the idea that a Jew who sins remains a Jew.

chat.says: Why does God say all Israel sinned when only Achan took the stuff?
options: Nobody here is purely private: what one person hides reaches everyone.
Because Achan was Israel's leader, so his sin counted for everyone.
Because Joshua had ordered the looting, so the blame fell on all.
chat.meaning: The text says Israel hath sinned though one man hid the goods: what one person buries reaches everyone, and the people keep their name.

notes: The confession sequence saw, coveted, took, hid follows 7:21; confirm against the JPS text.
The echo of 'hearts melted' (7:5 and Rahab's 2:11) is noted; confirm wording of both verses supports it.
Sanhedrin 44a ('even though he sinned, he is Israel') is paraphrased; confirm.
Valley of Achor glossed as 'trouble', following the text's own wordplay in 7:25–26; flag under the strict etymology rule.
The stoning of Achan and his household (7:24–25) is named briefly; a Keeper may want different wording.
